title: Auto-capture Discord opt-out bypass leaks captures
description: The new autoCaptureDiscordUploadEnabled helper returns true when either autoCapture.discord.enabled or the global output.uploadDiscord flag is set. finalizeAutoCaptureImage then uploads every auto-capture result and first prefers autoCapture.discord.webhookUrl before falling back to the primary Discord webhook. This means an existing or imported configuration with autoCapture.schedule.enabled=true, output.uploadDiscord=true, and autoCapture.discord.enabled=false will start posting scheduled/test auto-capture images after this update. If a stale or attacker-supplied autoCapture.discord.webhookUrl is present, it is used even though the auto-capture Discord feature is disabled. This can disclose VRChat capture images and configured Discord presence metadata to an unintended Discord webhook. Webhook URL validation still restricts the destination to Discord, so this is an information disclosure/consent bypass rather than arbitrary SSRF or code execution.

title: Unbounded CLI encryption can exhaust memory
description: This commit routes every startup argument that is not classified as an image extension into the new encryption flow before the UI starts. encryptPathWithPublicKey then handles any non-directory with os.ReadFile and handles directories by recursively walking them, deflating all files into an in-memory bytes.Buffer, returning the whole zip as []byte, and then encrypting that data into another in-memory bytes.Buffer. There is no maximum input size, total directory size, file count, recursion/depth bound, special-file rejection, or streaming to the output file. A malicious or simply very large non-image file/folder dragged onto ClipForVRChat.exe can therefore consume excessive RAM/CPU and crash or stall the application. The previous .zip encryption path already used memory buffering for zip files, but this commit substantially expands that behavior to arbitrary non-image files, folders, and multiple startup paths.

title: Raw issue quoting can leak user secrets
description: AGENTS.md now instructs contributors/agents to write the user's original statement exactly as-is into issue files. In this project, user reports may naturally include sensitive values such as Discord webhook URLs, webhook tokens, local paths, QR-code URLs, logs, config snippets, or diagnostic excerpts. Because issue files are committed into the repository and moved under issues/closed, this creates a durable disclosure path for bearer secrets and private data. The rule should require preserving user intent while redacting or replacing secrets and privacy-sensitive values before committing.

title: Unsaved draft can activate auto-post watchers
description: The commit adds automatic persistence and restoration of unsaved settings drafts. On startup, if a draft exists, main.go replaces state.Config with the draft and marks the UI as settings mode. However, when the app is launched with image arguments, it processes those images with the saved cfg variable, then overwrites state.Mode with results/error state without restoring state.Config back to the saved config or clearing the draft metadata. App.startup starts auto-photo/screenshot/auto-capture watchers whenever the final mode is ModeResults, using a.state.Config. Therefore a stale or malicious settings draft containing enabled AutoPhoto/ScreenshotAutoPost/AutoCapture settings and an attacker-controlled Discord webhook can be used as the runtime watcher configuration during a later image-processing launch, despite the user-facing message saying the draft is not applied to the settings file until saved. This can lead to unintended posting/exfiltration of newly watched VRChat photos or screenshots to the draft webhook. A safer design would keep restored drafts confined to settings UI state, reset state.Config to the saved cfg before entering results mode, or refuse to start background watchers while UnsavedSettingsDraft is true.

title: Hidden camera auto-start settings remain active
description: The frontend now hides the `openCameraBeforeBatch` and `closeCameraAfterBatch` controls from the auto-capture UI, but it only defaults them to false when they are undefined. If a user already had these fields set to true, or opens an attacker-supplied JSON config containing true values, the settings remain active with no normal UI control to review or disable them. The backend still uses these values to send OSC commands that open the VRChat camera, enable stream camera mode/streaming, and close the camera after capture. Combined with scheduled auto-capture and Discord auto-post settings, this can cause unexpected capture/posting behavior after a user saves an imported or stale config.

title: Diagnostic logs leak VRChat private instance IDs
description: This commit adds polling of VRChat output logs during capture-on-start readiness and writes the raw parsed world_id and instance_id to the diagnostic log when a candidate is seen or considered stable. VRChat instance IDs can include private instance details such as owner user IDs and nonce-like tokens (for example, private/hidden instance metadata). Diagnostic logs are included in the app's diagnostic package, and the plaintext ZIP intentionally remains for user review/sharing. The existing diagnostic redaction only removes known local paths and Discord webhook/token fields, so these newly logged world/instance identifiers survive into diagnostics. A remote attacker or support impersonator who convinces a user to share the diagnostic ZIP could learn where the user was in VRChat and potentially sensitive private instance metadata.

title: OSC forwarding can self-loop and cause UDP DoS
description: The commit adds UDP forwarding for received OSC packets and attempts to prevent forwarding to the receiver's own endpoint. However, sameOSCForwardEndpoint only treats an unspecified receive address as equivalent to nil, loopback, or another unspecified target. If the app is configured to listen on 0.0.0.0:<port> or [::]:<port>, a target such as the host's LAN IP on the same port is not considered self-forwarding. Because a UDP socket bound to 0.0.0.0:<port> receives packets sent to any local interface address on that port, the forwarder can send each received packet back to the same listener. The listener then reads the forwarded packet and forwards it again indefinitely. This can be triggered by any packet received on the exposed OSC port once such a configuration is active, causing CPU/network churn and log growth. The self-forward check should reject same-port targets for unspecified binds unless it can prove the target is not local, or it should enumerate local interface addresses and reject all local targets resolving to the receiver port.

title: Unbounded OSC packet logging enables log DoS
description: The OSC receiver is started during app startup and now writes a diagnostic log entry for every valid or invalid received UDP packet. The receiver accepts unauthenticated UDP datagrams, formats attacker-controlled address/type/value/payload data, and calls AppendDiagnosticLog for each packet. AppendDiagnosticLog appends to a dated log file with no rotation, quota, throttling, or maximum file size. Because the frontend exposes configurable OSC host/port and the backend uses that host for ListenUDP, exposure is loopback by default but can become network-adjacent if the user binds to a non-loopback or wildcard address. Even on default loopback, another local process can flood 127.0.0.1:9001. This can cause application slowdown from synchronous open/write/close per packet and unbounded disk consumption. Additionally, those logs are collected into diagnostic packages, so all captured OSC parameter names, values, payload hex previews, and remote addresses may be shared during support.

title: Auto-post warning suppressed when webhook is configured
description: Before this change, enabled VRChat photo and screenshot automatic processing were always included in the save confirmation, and the dialog told the user that matching images would be automatically processed and to verify the Discord destination. The new logic only adds confirmation items when Discord posting is enabled and the effective webhook is missing. Because the backend immediately restarts watchers after saving and auto-photo/screenshot/autocapture code falls back to the primary webhook, a configuration with auto processing enabled and a valid webhook no longer triggers this safety confirmation. This is security-relevant for untrusted or socially engineered configuration files: saving such a config can start background processing and upload future local images or autocapture output to the configured Discord webhook with less meaningful user visibility.

title: Unbounded OSC avatar parameter cache enables DoS
description: The commit adds avatar_osc basis handling to the OSC UDP receiver. Any OSC packet whose address starts with /avatar/parameters/ and has a supported scalar type is canonicalized and inserted into avatarOSCBasisSamples. There is no allow-list limiting storage to the configured basis parameter names, no cap on the number or length of cached addresses, no expiry/pruning, and rebuildAvatarOSCBasisLocked writes a diagnostic log entry for every accepted packet. A malicious local process, another local user, or an adjacent-network attacker if the OSC receiver is bound beyond loopback can send many unique avatar parameter addresses to grow the map indefinitely and/or send high-rate packets to grow diagnostic logs until memory or disk is exhausted. Because latestAvatarOSCSampleTime also scans all cached addresses by prefix, injected stale/junk prefixed parameters can keep avatar_osc basis stale and increase CPU work as the map grows.

title: Metadata failures can lead to unvalidated Discord uploads
description: In the parent commit, a failure from WriteAutoCaptureEmbeddedMetadata caused finalizeAutoCaptureImage to return before writing sidecars or uploading to Discord. This commit intentionally downgrades every metadata write error to a warning and continues. That is too broad: metadata write errors include unsupported or invalid image content. Photo-mode capture accepts new files from the watched directory based on extension and stability, not by decoding/validating the file. Later, uploadAutoCaptureDiscord reads the selected path directly and sends the raw bytes to Discord based only on the filename extension. As a result, if an attacker can place a newly modified .png/.jpg/.jpeg/.webp file in the watched VRChat photo/output directory during an auto-capture run, or can place a link/reparse point with such an extension to another readable file, the app may post those bytes to the configured Discord webhook despite the metadata writer having identified that the file is not a valid supported image. The safer behavior is to continue only for non-security metadata failures after validating that the file is a bounded, decodable image, or to keep aborting on format/parse failures.

title: Unbounded ZIP CLI encryption can exhaust memory
description: This commit adds a mode where launching the application with exactly one .zip argument encrypts that file and exits. The implementation only checks that the path has a .zip extension and is not a directory, then uses os.ReadFile to load the entire file into memory. It then validates the ZIP from the in-memory byte slice and encrypts into another in-memory buffer. A malicious or simply very large ZIP file can therefore force memory usage roughly proportional to the input plus encrypted output and ZIP metadata, potentially causing the process to hang, be killed, or destabilize the desktop session. The path is also not checked with info.Mode().IsRegular(), so special files such as FIFOs/devices on supported platforms could cause blocking or unbounded reads. This is introduced by the new CLI ZIP encryption path and should be mitigated by requiring a regular file, enforcing a maximum input size appropriate for diagnostic packages, and preferably streaming encryption instead of buffering the entire input and output.

title: Startup diagnostics log unredacted local paths
description: The new startup diagnostic flow records sensitive local filesystem paths in plaintext diagnostic.log on every UI startup. Although webhook URLs are reduced to boolean configured flags, the log still includes the full executable path, config path, history path, diagnostic log path, configured output directory, VRChat photo directory, and screenshot directory. These paths commonly contain the Windows username and may reveal private folder names, mounted/network paths, or user workflow details. Because diagnostic logs are intended for troubleshooting and may be requested or attached to GitHub issues/support discussions, this creates an information disclosure risk if a user shares the log or a diagnostic artifact containing it. The paths should be redacted or summarized before being written to a user-shareable diagnostic log.

title: Explorer reveal trusts history-controlled file paths
description: The commit adds a Wails-exposed RevealFileInExplorer(path) method. The backend only trims, absolutizes, stats, and rejects directories before launching explorer.exe with the supplied path. It does not verify that the path was produced by this app, is under the configured output directory, is a local file, or is an image. The frontend calls this API for any result item with outputPath, and resultItems falls back to visibleHistory when there are no current results. Since history.json is local JSON loaded into state without validating outputPath, a malicious imported config/history bundle or local history tampering can place an arbitrary existing path in outputPath. If the user clicks the new “保存先で表示” action, the app will os.Stat and then pass that path to Explorer. On Windows, this can be abused with attacker-controlled UNC paths to trigger SMB/WebDAV authentication and leak NetNTLM credentials, or to make Explorer open/select arbitrary non-output files and invoke shell/thumbnail handlers. The issue is not shell command injection because exec.Command separates arguments, but it is an authorization/validation flaw in a privileged filesystem bridge method.

title: Untrusted history paths are passed to Explorer
description: The commit adds RevealFileInExplorer(path) and wires result/history cards to call it with item.outputPath. The backend accepts any string from the renderer, resolves it to an absolute path, calls os.Stat on it, and then launches explorer.exe with /select,<path>. The frontend's resultItems are not only freshly generated processing results; when there are no current results, it maps entries from state.history directly into result cards. Because history.json is local JSON loaded without validating outputPath, a crafted or tampered history entry can supply an arbitrary local path or a Windows UNC path such as \\attacker.example\share\image.png. When the user clicks the new '保存先で表示' region, the app will probe that path and then ask Explorer to select it. On Windows, probing/opening UNC paths can initiate SMB/WebDAV authentication to an attacker-controlled host, leaking NetNTLM material, and the feature can also be abused as an arbitrary file/path probe/reveal primitive. The method should not accept arbitrary renderer paths; it should resolve by a trusted result/history ID, reject UNC/device paths, and ensure the canonical target is an app-created file under the configured output directory.

title: Hidden auto-processing folders can exfiltrate images
description: This commit removes the Auto Post settings tab and no longer renders controls for autoPhoto.photoDirectory, screenshotAutoPost.screenshotDirectory, or their scan intervals. Those fields still exist in config.json and are still used by restartAutoPhotoWatcher to start filesystem watchers. Because dropping/opening a JSON config loads that config into the settings flow, a malicious config can set uploadDiscord=true, autoPhoto.enabled or screenshotAutoPost.enabled=true, an attacker-controlled valid Discord webhook, and an arbitrary watch directory. The reorganized settings screen shows the auto-processing toggles and webhook fields but not the directory being monitored, so the user can save/activate a configuration that will upload future images from an attacker-chosen directory while believing only normal VRChat/Screenshots folders are involved.

title: Tabbed settings hide webhook auto-post settings
description: This commit changes the settings page from a single scrollable review to separate tabs and always resets new settings sessions to the Output tab. Sensitive destinations and background-upload controls, including the Discord webhook URL and VRChat/screenshot auto-post webhook settings, are now only rendered when their tabs are selected. However, the global Save button still sends the entire state.config object to the backend. If an attacker convinces a user to open and save a supplied config, the user can save attacker-controlled Discord and auto-post settings without ever seeing those fields. Saving then persists the configuration and restarts enabled auto-post watchers, which can upload future VRChat photos or screenshots to the configured Discord webhook. This is not a remote code execution issue and still requires user interaction, but it weakens review of security-sensitive imported settings and can lead to image exfiltration.

title: Screenshots can upload to the wrong Discord webhook
description: This commit adds screenshot auto-posting and documents it as using the normal Discord Webhook URL. However, the screenshot watcher in app.go only sets Directory and Interval, leaving WebhookURL empty. AutoPhotoWatcher.webhookURL() treats an empty explicit webhook as a signal to fall back to Config.AutoPhoto.WebhookURL. During processing, that fallback overwrites cfg.Discord.WebhookURL, so screenshots are uploaded to the VRChat auto-post webhook whenever it is configured. This can disclose sensitive desktop screenshots to an unintended Discord channel or an attacker-controlled webhook that the user only expected to receive VRChat photos.

title: Unvalidated update URL can open attacker-controlled links
description: This commit adds an update checker that fetches release metadata, copies the remote JSON html_url field into UpdateInfo.URL, exposes it to the frontend, and opens it through App.OpenURL when the update banner is clicked. App.OpenURL does not validate scheme, host, path, or protocol before calling BrowserOpenURL. If the GitHub API response is malicious, compromised, redirected to attacker-controlled JSON, or otherwise tampered with, the UI can present a trusted-looking update banner but open an arbitrary URL or custom protocol handler instead of the official GitHub Releases page. The update URL should be ignored in favor of a fixed official releases URL, or strictly validated to https://github.com/hatolife/ClipForVRChat/releases/... before being returned/opened; App.OpenURL should also enforce an allowlist defensively.

title: QR upscaling can exhaust memory on crafted tall images
description: This commit replaced the prior direct QR scan with DetectQRCodeURLsWithDiagnostics, which calls qrImageVariants before decoding. qrImageVariants creates 2x, 3x, and 4x resized copies, plus thresholded copies, whenever the original width is below 1800 or 900 pixels. It does not check height or resulting pixel count. The existing input validation only limits the original decoded image to MaxImagePixels. For example, an attacker-supplied 800x80000 PNG is exactly 64,000,000 pixels and can be highly compressed under the byte limit, but QR detection will attempt to allocate variants up to 3200x320000, over one billion pixels, and additional threshold copies. This can cause out-of-memory termination or severe UI/processing denial of service when a user processes the image or when it appears in a watched photo folder with QR detection enabled.

title: Untrusted QR URLs can trigger Discord mentions
description: QR payloads are treated as safe if they parse as an http/https URL with a hostname, then the original raw string is concatenated into the Discord message body. Go's URL parser accepts strings such as URLs containing raw Discord mention tokens in the path or query, for example `https://example.com/<@&123456789012345678>`. The webhook payload only sets `content` and does not set `allowed_mentions`, so Discord's default mention parsing can allow a malicious QR code in an image to ping users, roles, or everyone in the configured Discord channel when the user processes the image or when auto-photo processing handles it.

title: Unbounded native clipboard PNG copy can crash app
description: This commit adds a Windows-specific path that prefers registered clipboard formats named "PNG" or "image/png". After opening the clipboard, it calls GlobalSize on the clipboard handle and immediately creates and copies a Go byte slice of that full size. The existing MaxInputMB validation is only reached later in DecodeImageWithLimit, after ReadClipboardImage has already returned the copied bytes. A local process, or an attacker who convinces the user to place specially crafted registered PNG data on the clipboard and then click the clipboard processing button, can provide a very large HGLOBAL for the PNG format. The app will attempt to allocate and copy that entire buffer before rejecting it, causing memory exhaustion or a fatal crash. The new native path should enforce the configured/default maximum byte limit before unsafe.Slice and make/copy, or stream/copy only up to a bounded limit and fail if GlobalSize exceeds that bound.

title: Auto-photo scan cap can leak old photos and starve new ones
description: The commit limits auto-photo scanning to the first MaxAutoPhotoScanFiles supported paths discovered by WalkDir. AutoPhotoWatcher.Run initializes w.seen from this limited result, not from the full directory. As a result, in a watched directory with more than 5000 supported image paths, all existing files after the cutoff are absent from the startup baseline. If earlier files are deleted or an attacker removes lexicographically early filler files, previously existing user photos can enter the limited scan result, appear absent from w.seen, and be processed as if they were newly created. Auto-photo processing forces Discord upload, so this can disclose older local photos to the configured webhook without the user's intent. Conversely, an attacker who can create 5000 lexicographically early supported filenames in the watched folder can keep genuine later photos permanently outside the scan result, causing feature-level denial of service.

title: History file stores Discord tokens with weak permissions
description: The new history feature persists Discord deletion metadata, including DiscordWebhookID, DiscordToken, and DiscordMessageID, for every successful upload. SaveHistory writes history.json with mode 0644 and creates its parent directory with 0755, making the file readable by other local users on platforms where POSIX modes apply and by any process/account that can access the app directory. A reader of this file can recover Discord webhook bearer tokens plus message IDs for historical uploads, enabling unauthorized posting to the webhook and deletion of recorded Discord messages. The data is also included in UI state/results even though the frontend only needs opaque history IDs to request deletion, increasing exposure to any renderer compromise or accidental state disclosure.
